newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Ecopetrol eyes large oil reserves.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Ecopetrol eyes large oil reserves.

text.p: Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol is adopting a more adventurous policy in exploring large oil reserves, its chairman Luis Bernardo Florez said on Sunday.

In an interview with Caracol radio, Florez said the discovery of the Coporo site, 55 miles (90 km) east of Bogota, announced by President Ernesto Samper in New York last week, reflected such a policy.
"In the past, Ecopetrol has concentrated on less expensive exploration projects where the possibility of big finds was much less," he said.
"But we've taken this big step to find larger reserves even though it costs more. We're aware of the risks but we can prove that Ecopetrol now wears long trousers in terms of exploration."
Florez said Ecopetrol would welcome foreign investment and technology as they were vital to the development of the key oil sector.
While in New York to address the United Nations, Samper said the Coporo site, on the eastern plains, held 700 million barrels.

But in Sunday's radio interview, Florez repeated earlier statements that no accurate predictions about the potential size of reserves would be available until a test well was completed in December. He reconfirmed geologists estimates that Coporo could top 1.3 billion barrels.
Samper's optimism about the size of the find came after a rift in Ecopetrol's board of directors.

Jose Fernando Isaza, a veteran member, quit on September 9 in protest at what he described as undue pressure to change British Petroleum Co Plc's association contract to explore the Piedmonte area, not far from Coporo.

Under the sliding-scale formula, BP's payments to Ecopetrol increase in line with rising output, to a maximum of 76 percent of profits. BP argues in the competitive international climate and given the depth of the reserves, between 15,000 and 18,000 feet, that the margins are not attractive enough.

In a move unlikely to appease the powerful USO oil union, angered by what it sees as BP's bid to take advantage of the prolonged political crisis, Florez hinted that Colombia was ready to bend to foreign oil companies' demands.

"Other countries previously closed to foreign venture capital are now vying for that money so each country must now make bigger efforts to attract what foreign capital is available. We will continue looking at the international climate and see if we need to make additional changes in (oil contracts)," Florez said.
Colombia's proven oil reserves currently stand at 3.1 billion barrels but the government expects that figure to grow to nine billion barrels by the year 2010.
